stories.title: Trade hubs, Dilmun to New York
stories.blurb: Which ports and markets sat at the centre of world trade, and why did the centre keep moving?

steps.name: Dilmun
steps.what: Inscriptions of Sargon of Akkad boast that ships from Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha moored at the quay of his capital; Dilmun, on Bahrain, was the go-between for Mesopotamian grain and Omani copper and Indus goods.
steps.why: The first trade hub we can name was an island with fresh springs halfway down the Gulf, a middleman between richer neighbours.

steps.name: Ugarit
steps.what: Ugarit's harbour at Minet el-Beida linked Egypt, the Hittites, Cyprus and Mesopotamia, and its scribes kept archives in several languages and wrote a 30-sign cuneiform alphabet.
steps.why: A Bronze Age port grew rich by sitting where empires met; it was destroyed around 1185 BCE in the Late Bronze Age collapse.

steps.name: Hiram I of Tyre
steps.what: King Hiram I of Tyre traded cedar and craftsmen to Solomon of Israel for farm produce, and Tyrian ships began the Phoenician trade network that later founded Carthage and Gades.
steps.why: Tyre turned a small island city into the hub of a sea network spanning the whole Mediterranean.

steps.name: Founding of Alexandria
steps.what: Alexander the Great founded Alexandria on the coast west of the Nile delta; under the Ptolemies it became the largest port of the Mediterranean, shipping Egyptian grain and Indian goods.
steps.why: Alexandria joined the Mediterranean to the Nile and the Red Sea routes, and stayed a leading port for nearly a thousand years.

steps.name: Tang Chang'an
steps.what: Tang Chang'an, a walled grid of about 84 square kilometres, had an East Market and a West Market where Sogdian, Persian and Uyghur merchants sold horses, silver, spices and silk.
steps.why: The eastern end of the Silk Roads was probably the largest city in the world, drawing trade across Asia by land.

steps.name: Founding of Baghdad
steps.what: The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founded his Round City on the Tigris, near where the Tigris and Euphrates come closest, and within decades Baghdad was the largest city of the Islamic world.
steps.why: Baghdad sat where river routes from the Gulf met caravan roads, making it the centre of trade between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean.

steps.name: Venice mints the ducat
steps.what: Under Doge Giovanni Dandolo Venice began minting a gold ducat of about 3.5 grams, which kept its weight and purity for five centuries.
steps.why: A trusted coin and state-run convoys to Alexandria and the Black Sea made Venice the hub of Europe's trade with the East.

steps.name: Founding of the Malacca Sultanate
steps.what: Parameswara, a prince from Sumatra, founded Malacca on the strait; Ming fleets under Zheng He visited from 1405 and backed the new port against Siam.
steps.why: Malacca controlled the narrow strait every ship between India and China had to pass, and waited there for the monsoon to turn.

steps.name: Antwerp Bourse opens
steps.what: Antwerp opened a purpose-built exchange building where merchants from across Europe traded bills and commodities, while Portuguese spices and German silver met in the city.
steps.why: Antwerp became the hub of Europe's first global trade, before war and the Spanish sack of 1576 drove merchants north.

steps.name: Founding of the Dutch East India Company
steps.what: The States General chartered the Dutch East India Company (VOC), whose shares, with the Amsterdam chamber holding about half the capital, were traded on a permanent market in Amsterdam.
steps.why: Amsterdam combined shipping, cheap credit and a share market, and ran the spice trade for most of the 17th century.

steps.name: West India Docks open
steps.what: The West India Docks opened on the Isle of Dogs, the first of London's enclosed wet docks, built to unload sugar and rum safely away from river thieves.
steps.why: London's docks, insurers and banks made it the centre of world trade in the 19th century.

steps.name: 1819 Singapore Treaty
steps.what: Stamford Raffles signed a treaty with Sultan Hussein Shah and the Temenggong of Johor letting the British East India Company set up a trading post at Singapore, run as a free port.
steps.why: Singapore took over Malacca's old role at the strait, and free trade made it a hub within a few decades.

steps.name: Opening of the Erie Canal
steps.what: Governor DeWitt Clinton poured Lake Erie water into New York harbour to mark the completion of the 584 km Erie Canal from Buffalo to the Hudson.
steps.why: The canal made New York the cheapest gateway to the American interior, and it soon passed every other American port.

stories.title: The seven wonders, built and lost
stories.blurb: When were the seven wonders of the ancient world built, and what destroyed six of them?

steps.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
steps.what: The pharaoh Khufu's pyramid was built of about 2.3 million stone blocks to a height of about 146 metres.
steps.why: The oldest wonder is the only one still standing; it was the tallest building in the world for almost 4,000 years.

steps.name: Hanging Gardens of Babylon
steps.what: Greek writers said Nebuchadnezzar II built terraced gardens watered by machines in Babylon, but no Babylonian text mentions them and no trace has been found.
steps.why: The only wonder whose existence is doubted; some scholars think the story describes Sennacherib's gardens at Nineveh.

steps.name: Temple of Artemis rebuilt
steps.what: King Croesus of Lydia paid for much of a huge marble temple to Artemis at Ephesus, with more than a hundred columns.
steps.why: The temple was a shrine and a bank for the Ionian world, and Greek writers rated it above the other wonders.

steps.name: Statue of Zeus at Olympia
steps.what: The sculptor Phidias made a seated Zeus about 12 metres tall in gold and ivory for the temple at Olympia, home of the Olympic Games.
steps.why: The most famous cult statue of the Greek world stood for about eight centuries.

steps.name: Herostratus burns the Temple of Artemis
steps.what: A man named Herostratus set fire to the Temple of Artemis to make himself famous; the Ephesians later rebuilt it on the same plan.
steps.why: The first wonder lost was destroyed by one man's arson, though it was rebuilt.

steps.name: Mausoleum at Halicarnassus
steps.what: The tomb of Mausolus, ruler of Caria, finished under his widow Artemisia, rose about 45 metres with sculpture by four leading Greek artists.
steps.why: It gave the word 'mausoleum' to every language in Europe.

steps.name: Colossus of Rhodes
steps.what: Chares of Lindos finished a bronze statue of the sun god Helios about 33 metres tall, paid for by selling siege equipment left behind by Demetrius I.
steps.why: Rhodes built its wonder to celebrate surviving a siege of 305-304 BCE.

steps.name: Lighthouse of Alexandria
steps.what: On the island of Pharos the Ptolemies built a lighthouse more than 100 metres tall, often credited to the architect Sostratus of Cnidus.
steps.why: The last wonder built was also the most useful: it guided grain ships into the busiest harbour of the Mediterranean.

steps.name: Colossus falls in an earthquake
steps.what: An earthquake snapped the Colossus at the knees; the Rhodians declined to rebuild it and the ruins lay on the ground for about 800 years.
steps.why: The shortest-lived wonder stood for only about 54 years.

steps.name: Antipater of Sidon's list
steps.what: The poet Antipater of Sidon wrote an epigram naming seven sights, close to the list we use today, though with the walls of Babylon instead of the lighthouse.
steps.why: The 'seven wonders' were a Greek tourist list, written down after one of them had already fallen.

steps.name: Goths sack the Temple of Artemis
steps.what: Gothic raiders sacked Ephesus and damaged the temple; it was not restored, and in the Christian era its stones were carried off for other buildings.
steps.why: War and then religious change finished the temple.

steps.name: Statue of Zeus destroyed
steps.what: According to one account the statue, moved to a palace in Constantinople, burned in a great fire in 475; others say it perished at Olympia.
steps.why: The pagan temples were closed and their treasures removed or lost.

steps.name: 1303 Crete earthquake
steps.what: A strong earthquake in the eastern Mediterranean, with a tsunami, badly damaged the Pharos, already weakened by earlier quakes.
steps.why: Earthquakes, not war, brought down the lighthouse after about 1,600 years.

steps.name: Citadel of Qaitbay
steps.what: The Mamluk sultan Qaitbay built a fort on the lighthouse site, reusing some of its fallen stone.
steps.why: The last trace of the lighthouse above ground was folded into a fort.

steps.name: Mausoleum stones used for Bodrum Castle
steps.what: The Knights Hospitaller took stone from the Mausoleum, already ruined by earthquakes, to strengthen their Castle of St Peter against the Ottomans.
steps.why: Of the seven, only the Great Pyramid remained; the rest were lost to earthquakes, fire, raids and reuse.

stories.title: Lost cities and why they died
stories.blurb: Great cities have been emptied by war, rivers that moved, failing trade and changing climate; which killed which?

steps.name: Decline of Mohenjo-daro
steps.what: The planned brick city of perhaps 40,000 people on the Indus, with drains and a great bath, was gradually abandoned.
steps.why: No conqueror is needed to explain it; shifting rivers and a weaker monsoon are the leading explanations.

steps.name: Burning of Persepolis
steps.what: After taking the Persian ceremonial capital, Alexander's army looted it and burned the palace of Xerxes.
steps.why: Persepolis died with the empire that built it; it had no other reason to exist.

steps.name: Babylon emptied for Seleucia
steps.what: The Seleucid king Antiochus I moved many of Babylon's people to the new capital of Seleucia on the Tigris.
steps.why: Babylon was not destroyed in one blow; it faded as power and trade moved to a new city.

steps.name: Siege of Carthage
steps.what: A Roman army under Scipio Aemilianus stormed Carthage after a three-year siege, burned it and sold about 50,000 survivors into slavery.
steps.why: A rival city was wiped out on purpose; Rome later refounded it as a Roman colony.

steps.name: Aurelian sacks Palmyra
steps.what: After Queen Zenobia's breakaway empire was defeated, Palmyra revolted again and the emperor Aurelian's troops sacked it.
steps.why: A caravan city lived on desert trade between Rome and Persia; once punished it never regained that trade.

steps.name: Burning of central Teotihuacan
steps.what: The ceremonial centre of Teotihuacan, a city of perhaps 100,000 or more, was burned and the city declined over the following century.
steps.why: The burning seems targeted at elite buildings, so internal revolt, perhaps after drought, is a leading theory.

steps.name: Abandonment of Uruk
steps.what: Uruk, one of the first true cities, was finally abandoned after more than 4,000 years.
steps.why: The Euphrates shifted away from the city, leaving its fields without water.
steps.date_note: c.; abandoned around the Islamic conquest of 633-638

steps.name: Mongol destruction of Merv
steps.what: Merv, one of the largest cities of Central Asia, surrendered to Tolui's Mongol army and its people were massacred; chroniclers claimed hundreds of thousands of dead.
steps.why: Merv's irrigation needed many hands; with the people killed the oasis city never recovered its size.

steps.name: Abandonment of Cahokia
steps.what: Cahokia, a Mississippian city near modern St Louis with tens of thousands of people at its peak around 1100 and the huge Monks Mound, was empty by about 1350.
steps.why: Floods, drought, exhausted wood and soil, and political trouble are all proposed; the cause is still debated.

steps.name: Ayutthaya sacks Angkor
steps.what: The Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya sacked Angkor and the Khmer court moved south towards Phnom Penh.
steps.why: War was the last blow to a city whose vast water system was already strained by droughts and floods.

steps.name: Abandonment of Great Zimbabwe
steps.what: The stone city of perhaps 18,000 people, rich from gold traded to the coast at Kilwa, was largely abandoned.
steps.why: Trade routes moved north and the land around the city may have been exhausted.

steps.name: Battle of Talikota
steps.what: An alliance of the Deccan sultanates defeated the army of Vijayanagara, then looted the capital for months.
steps.why: One of the largest cities in the world was ruined within a year by a single defeat.

stories.title: The Silk Roads over two thousand years
stories.blurb: How did the overland routes between China and the West open, carry goods and ideas, and fade?

steps.name: Zhang Qian sets out
steps.what: The Han emperor Wu sent Zhang Qian west to find allies against the Xiongnu; he was captured and held for about ten years.
steps.why: The first known Chinese envoy to Central Asia opened official contact with the west.

steps.name: Zhang Qian in Bactria
steps.what: After escaping, Zhang Qian reached Ferghana and Bactria, saw Chinese goods for sale there, and returned home in 126 BCE with reports of fine horses.
steps.why: His reports convinced the Han court that trade and alliances in the west were worth pursuing.

steps.name: War of the Heavenly Horses
steps.what: The general Li Guangli led Han armies against Dayuan in Ferghana to win its horses, succeeding on the second attempt.
steps.why: China projected power into Central Asia to secure the routes and the horses it needed.

steps.name: Sogdian Ancient Letters
steps.what: Sogdian merchants in China wrote letters home to Samarkand describing the fall of Luoyang; the undelivered letters were found in a watchtower near Dunhuang in 1907.
steps.why: Sogdians, not Chinese or Romans, carried most of the overland trade.

steps.name: Mogao Caves begun
steps.what: According to tradition a monk began carving Buddhist cave shrines into a cliff near Dunhuang, the oasis where routes split around the Taklamakan.
steps.why: The roads carried religion as well as goods; Buddhism reached China this way.

steps.name: Xuanzang passes Samarkand
steps.what: The Chinese monk Xuanzang, travelling to India for Buddhist texts, passed through Samarkand, the chief Sogdian city.
steps.why: Pilgrims used the same roads and caravanserais as merchants.

steps.name: Battle of Talas
steps.what: An Abbasid army, helped by the Karluk Turks, defeated a Tang army under Gao Xianzhi on the Talas river.
steps.why: It marked the western limit of Chinese power; tradition says captured Chinese papermakers brought paper to Samarkand.

steps.name: An Lushan rebellion
steps.what: An Lushan, a Tang general of Sogdian and Turkic descent, rebelled; the war cost millions of lives and the Tang pulled troops out of Central Asia.
steps.why: China lost control of the western routes for centuries.

steps.name: Paper made in Baghdad
steps.what: Baghdad's first paper mill was set up under the Abbasids, spreading a Chinese technology that came west along the Silk Roads.
steps.why: The most important thing the routes carried may have been an idea, not silk.

steps.name: Marco Polo reaches Kublai Khan
steps.what: The Venetian Marco Polo, with his father and uncle, reached Kublai Khan's summer capital after crossing Asia overland.
steps.why: Under Mongol rule the whole route lay in one family's empire, and Europeans could travel it.

steps.name: Siege of Caffa
steps.what: Plague struck the Golden Horde army of Jani Beg besieging the Genoese port of Caffa, and Genoese ships carried the disease to the Mediterranean.
steps.why: The same connected world that carried trade carried the Black Death, which helped break the Mongol order.

steps.name: Clavijo at Timur's court
steps.what: The Castilian envoy Ruy González de Clavijo reached Samarkand, which Timur was rebuilding with craftsmen taken from conquered cities.
steps.why: Samarkand had a last great age as a land-route capital.

steps.name: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut
steps.what: The Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama reached India by sailing round Africa.
steps.why: Sea routes could carry far more for less, and over the next centuries the overland caravans lost their long-distance trade.

steps.name: Bento de Góis reaches China
steps.what: The Jesuit Bento de Góis travelled overland from India to the edge of China and confirmed that 'Cathay' and China were the same place; he died there in 1607.
steps.why: By then the old road was so little used that Europeans had to check where it led.

steps.name: Richthofen names the Silk Road
steps.what: The geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen used the term 'Seidenstraße' (Silk Road) in his work on China.
steps.why: The name is modern: the travellers themselves never called it that.

steps.name: Aurel Stein at Dunhuang
steps.what: Aurel Stein bought thousands of manuscripts from a sealed cave at Mogao from the caretaker Wang Yuanlu, including the Diamond Sutra of 868, the oldest dated printed book.
steps.why: The routes' history was recovered from their ruins, and much of it was carried off to Europe.

stories.title: The monsoon ocean
stories.blurb: How did the seasonal monsoon winds tie Africa, Arabia, India and Southeast Asia into one trading world, and who tried to control it?

steps.name: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
steps.what: A Greek-speaking merchant in Roman Egypt wrote a guide to ports from the Red Sea to India, noting what to buy and sell and when the monsoon winds blew.
steps.why: Sailors timed voyages to the winds: south-west to India in summer, north-east back in winter.

steps.name: Muziris papyrus
steps.what: A loan contract written in Egypt covered a cargo of pepper, ivory and textiles shipped from Muziris on the Malabar coast in the ship Hermapollon.
steps.why: Roman money paid for Indian pepper on a large scale.

steps.name: Kedukan Bukit inscription
steps.what: An inscription at Palembang records an expedition by the ruler Dapunta Hyang with an army of 20,000, the earliest record of Srivijaya.
steps.why: Srivijaya grew by controlling the straits between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea.

steps.name: Belitung shipwreck
steps.what: An Arab-style sewn ship sank off Belitung carrying about 60,000 pieces of Tang Chinese ceramics, gold and silver.
steps.why: Ships sailed directly between China and the Persian Gulf, a two-way trade that the wreck proves.

steps.name: Chola invasion of Srivijaya
steps.what: The Chola king Rajendra I sent a fleet across the Bay of Bengal that raided Srivijaya's ports, including Kadaram in Kedah.
steps.why: The ocean's trade was rich enough for an Indian kingdom to fight for it overseas.

steps.name: Ibn Battuta at Kilwa
steps.what: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta visited Kilwa and called it one of the most beautiful cities in the world; its sultans grew rich on gold from Great Zimbabwe.
steps.why: The Swahili coast linked the African interior to the ocean trade.

steps.name: Zheng He at Calicut
steps.what: The Ming admiral Zheng He's first treasure fleet, with dozens of large ships, reached Calicut on the Malabar coast.
steps.why: China showed it could dominate the ocean, then chose to stop after 1433.

steps.name: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut
steps.what: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut after sailing round Africa, guided across the Arabian Sea from Malindi by a local pilot.
steps.why: Europeans entered a trading world that already existed, and soon used guns to tax it.

steps.name: Portuguese conquest of Hormuz
steps.what: Afonso de Albuquerque attacked Hormuz, the island at the mouth of the Persian Gulf; Portugal secured it fully in 1515.
steps.why: Hormuz was one of the chokepoints Portugal needed to control the ocean's trade.

steps.name: Portuguese conquest of Goa
steps.what: Albuquerque took Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate, and it became the capital of the Portuguese State of India.
steps.why: Portugal built a network of fortified ports and sold passes to Asian ships.

steps.name: Capture of Malacca
steps.what: Albuquerque's fleet captured Malacca, the richest port of the straits.
steps.why: Taking the strait gave Portugal a hold on the spice trade, though Asian merchants moved to other ports.

steps.name: Said bin Sultan moves to Zanzibar
steps.what: Sultan Said bin Sultan of Oman moved his capital to Zanzibar, which grew rich on clove plantations and the ivory and slave trades.
steps.why: The monsoon still carried Arab dhows between Oman and East Africa, often in human cargo.

steps.name: Opening of the Suez Canal
steps.what: The Suez Canal opened, joining the Mediterranean to the Red Sea.
steps.why: Steamships through Suez no longer had to wait for the monsoon or round Africa, ending the age of sail in the ocean.

stories.title: The industrial revolution in Britain
stories.blurb: How did coal, steam, cotton and rail turn Britain into the first industrial economy between 1709 and 1851?

steps.name: Darby smelts iron with coke
steps.what: Abraham Darby I made iron in a blast furnace fuelled by coke from coal instead of charcoal from wood.
steps.why: Iron no longer depended on forests, and coal became the base of industry.

steps.name: Newcomen's first engine
steps.what: Thomas Newcomen built the first working steam engine near Dudley Castle to pump water out of coal mines.
steps.why: Steam first earned its keep by helping dig more coal.

steps.name: Bridgewater Canal opens
steps.what: The Duke of Bridgewater's canal, engineered by James Brindley, carried coal from his Worsley mines to Manchester and halved its price there.
steps.why: Cheap transport for heavy goods set off a canal boom.

steps.name: Cromford Mill
steps.what: Richard Arkwright built a water-powered cotton spinning mill at Cromford, run in shifts by hundreds of workers, many of them children.
steps.why: This is often called the first modern factory: machines, power and discipline under one roof.

steps.name: Boulton and Watt
steps.what: James Watt joined Matthew Boulton at Soho, Birmingham, to build steam engines with Watt's separate condenser, which used far less coal than Newcomen's.
steps.why: Efficient steam power could be used away from coalfields and, after 1781, to turn machines.

steps.name: The Iron Bridge
steps.what: Abraham Darby III cast the world's first major iron bridge across the Severn; it opened in 1781.
steps.why: Cheap iron could now build things that were once made of wood and stone.

steps.name: Murrays' Mills
steps.what: The Murray brothers began large steam-powered cotton mills in Ancoats, Manchester, one of the first areas packed with mills.
steps.why: Steam let mills cluster in towns, and Manchester grew into 'Cottonopolis'.

steps.name: Luddite machine-breaking
steps.what: Stocking knitters broke wide knitting frames in Arnold and nearby villages, starting the Luddite movement.
steps.why: Workers whose skills machines made worthless fought back; the government sent thousands of troops.

steps.name: Peterloo Massacre
steps.what: Cavalry charged a crowd of about 60,000 gathered at St Peter's Field to hear Henry Hunt call for parliamentary reform; at least 15 died and hundreds were hurt.
steps.why: Industrial towns had grown huge but had no MPs, and the demand for a vote came from them.

steps.name: Stockton and Darlington Railway opens
steps.what: George Stephenson's locomotive Locomotion No. 1 hauled coal wagons and passengers on the first public railway to use steam locomotives.
steps.why: Railways began as another way to move coal cheaply.

steps.name: Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens
steps.what: The first intercity railway, fully steam-hauled and double tracked, opened; the MP William Huskisson was killed by the Rocket on opening day.
steps.why: Linking the cotton port to the cotton town began the railway age.

steps.name: Factory Act 1833
steps.what: Parliament banned work by children under nine in textile mills, limited the hours of older children, and appointed factory inspectors.
steps.why: The state began to regulate the factory system.

steps.name: Great Exhibition
who: Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha
steps.what: Six million visitors came to Joseph Paxton's iron-and-glass Crystal Palace to see machines and goods from around the world, about half the space given to Britain and its empire.
steps.why: Britain showed off its lead as the workshop of the world.

stories.title: The Belle Époque
stories.blurb: What did Europe's long peace between 1871 and 1914 produce, and how did it end?

steps.name: Semaine sanglante
steps.what: French government troops retook Paris from the Commune in a week of street fighting and executions; thousands of Communards were killed.
steps.why: The Belle Époque began in the ashes of civil war and defeat by Prussia.

steps.name: First Impressionist exhibition
steps.what: Thirty artists rejected by the official Salon showed their work in the photographer Nadar's former studio; a critic mocked Monet's Impression, Sunrise and named the movement.
steps.why: Painting turned to modern city life and light, outside official taste.

steps.name: First Bayreuth Festival
steps.what: Richard Wagner opened his own theatre at Bayreuth with the first full performance of The Ring of the Nibelung.
steps.why: The new German empire had its own cultural pilgrimage.

steps.name: Exposition Universelle (1889)
steps.what: The world's fair for the centenary of the Revolution opened under Gustave Eiffel's 300-metre iron tower, then the tallest structure in the world; about 32 million visits followed.
steps.why: France displayed its recovery, its engineering and its empire.

steps.name: Moulin Rouge opens
steps.what: The Moulin Rouge cabaret opened at the foot of Montmartre and made the cancan famous.
steps.why: Paris nightlife became an industry and an image of the age.

steps.name: Lumière brothers' first public screening
steps.what: Auguste and Louis Lumière showed ten short films to a paying audience in the basement of the Grand Café.
steps.why: Cinema was born as public entertainment.

steps.name: Vienna Secession
steps.what: Gustav Klimt and other artists left Vienna's official artists' association to found the Secession, with its own exhibition hall from 1898.
steps.why: Vienna became a second capital of modern art and design.

steps.name: J'Accuse...!
steps.what: Émile Zola published an open letter in L'Aurore accusing the army of convicting the Jewish officer Alfred Dreyfus of treason on false evidence.
steps.why: The peace hid deep conflict over antisemitism, the army and the Republic.

steps.name: Paris Métro opens
steps.what: The first Paris Métro line opened between Porte de Vincennes and Porte Maillot during the 1900 world's fair, with entrances designed by Hector Guimard.
steps.why: Electric transport changed daily life in the great cities.

steps.name: Entente Cordiale
steps.what: Britain and France settled their colonial disputes in a set of agreements.
steps.why: Old rivals lined up together, forming one side of the alliance system that would go to war.

steps.name: First Ballets Russes season
steps.what: Sergei Diaghilev's Russian company opened its first Paris season of ballet.
steps.why: Paris became the meeting place of the European avant-garde.

steps.name: Premiere of The Rite of Spring
steps.what: Stravinsky's score and Nijinsky's choreography for the Ballets Russes caused uproar in the audience on the first night.
steps.why: The age's own art was already breaking with its manners.

steps.name: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
steps.what: The Bosnian Serb student Gavrilo Princip shot the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne and his wife.
steps.why: The shooting set off the July Crisis.

steps.name: Assassination of Jean Jaurès
steps.what: The socialist leader Jean Jaurès, who was trying to stop the war, was shot dead in a café by a nationalist.
steps.why: The best-known voice for peace in France was silenced on the eve of war.

steps.name: Germany declares war on France
steps.what: Germany declared war on France, two days after both countries ordered general mobilisation, and invaded Belgium the next day.
steps.why: The long peace ended in a war that killed millions and swept away the world it had built.

stories.title: Great powers, 1000 to 2000
stories.blurb: Who was the strongest power in each age of the second millennium, where was its centre, and what made it strong?

steps.name: Song Kaifeng
steps.what: The Song capital Kaifeng, a commercial city with perhaps a million people, sat on canals that brought rice and goods from the south.
steps.why: Song China led the world in rice yields, iron output, printing and the use of paper money.

steps.name: Walls of Karakorum
steps.what: Ögedei Khan walled the Mongol capital Karakorum, where envoys and merchants from Europe to China came to the court.
steps.why: Mounted archers, discipline and a relay-post system built the largest land empire ever.

steps.name: Forbidden City completed
steps.what: The Yongle Emperor completed the Forbidden City and made Beijing the Ming capital the next year, while Zheng He's fleets sailed to Africa.
steps.why: A rebuilt state with a huge population, the Grand Canal and the largest fleet of its day.

steps.name: Casa de Contratación
steps.what: Spain set up the Casa de Contratación in Seville to control all trade and shipping with the Americas.
steps.why: American conquests gave Spain an empire on several continents.

steps.name: Silver of Potosí
steps.what: Silver was found at the Cerro Rico; worked by forced indigenous labour, Potosí became one of the largest cities in the Americas.
steps.why: American silver paid for Spain's armies and flowed on to China.

steps.name: Süleymaniye Mosque
steps.what: The architect Mimar Sinan finished the great mosque of Suleiman the Magnificent above the Golden Horn.
steps.why: The Ottomans held three continents, with a strong standing army, gunpowder and control of key trade routes.

steps.name: Founding of Fatehpur Sikri
steps.what: The Mughal emperor Akbar began a new red sandstone capital at Fatehpur Sikri.
steps.why: Mughal India was among the largest economies in the world, rich in textiles and land taxes.

steps.name: Bank of Amsterdam
steps.what: Amsterdam founded an exchange bank that gave merchants reliable money for settling bills.
steps.why: The Dutch Republic was small but led in shipping, finance and trade.

steps.name: Macartney Embassy
steps.what: The Qianlong Emperor received Lord Macartney's British embassy at Chengde but refused its requests for more trade.
steps.why: Qing China, at its largest extent and with about 300 million people, did not think it needed Britain.

steps.name: Battle of Trafalgar
steps.what: Nelson's fleet of 27 ships defeated 33 French and Spanish ships off southern Spain; Nelson was killed.
steps.why: British sea power went unchallenged for a century.

steps.name: Diamond Jubilee of Queen Victoria
steps.what: Troops from across the British Empire paraded through London for Queen Victoria's 60 years on the throne.
steps.why: Industry, the navy and the City of London ran an empire covering about a fifth of the world's land.

steps.name: Moving assembly line
steps.what: Ford introduced the moving assembly line for the Model T at Highland Park, cutting the time to build a car from about twelve hours to about an hour and a half.
steps.why: Mass production and a huge home market made the United States the largest industrial economy.

steps.name: Bretton Woods Conference
steps.what: Delegates from 44 countries set up the IMF and World Bank and a post-war money system pegged to the US dollar.
steps.why: The United States came out of the war with most of the world's gold and much of its industry.

steps.name: Sputnik 1
steps.what: The Soviet Union launched the first artificial satellite.
steps.why: Planned heavy industry and science made the USSR the second superpower.

steps.name: Shenzhen Special Economic Zone
steps.what: China created a special economic zone at Shenzhen, then a small town next to Hong Kong, open to foreign investment.
steps.why: China's reforms began the return of the world's largest population to economic power.

steps.name: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
steps.what: The Soviet Union formally ceased to exist, a day after Mikhail Gorbachev resigned.
steps.why: The century ended with one superpower, the United States.
